content.text: What Drives the Cost of a Kitchen Remodel?
In our experience across hundreds of Richmond-area kitchens, five factors consistently move the needle most:

items: Cabinets (40–50% of total budget): Stock cabinets run $60–$200/linear ft installed. Semi-custom is $150–$400. Custom can exceed $500/linear ft.

Appliances: A basic package (range, fridge, dishwasher) starts at $3,500. Mid-range is $6,000–$12,000. Luxury brands (Wolf, Sub-Zero, Miele) can exceed $25,000.
Labor: Richmond-area labor rates for kitchen remodels range from $50–$90/hr depending on trade. Electrical and plumbing add $3,000–$8,000 for a typical reconfiguration.
Structural changes: Moving walls, relocating the sink, or expanding the kitchen footprint adds $5,000–$20,000+. In Chesterfield County, moving, adding, or removing a wall requires a building permit.

content.text: Richmond-Specific Cost Factors

Older homes in neighborhoods like Forest Hill, Bon Air, and the Westover Hills area often have aging plumbing (cast iron, galvanized) and knob-and-tube or early aluminum wiring that is usually replaced once the walls are opened for new electrical or plumbing work. A typical kitchen remodel that touches electrical and plumbing lands around $230 to $350 in county fees. Replacing cabinets, plumbing fixtures like sinks and faucets, and floor coverings does not require a permit by itself. We handle the entire permit process, so you don't have to deal with any of it.

title: Do I Need a Permit to Build a Deck in Chesterfield County, VA?
metaTitle: Deck Permit Chesterfield County VA — What You Need to Know | MAS Contractors
metaDescription: Find out when a deck permit is required in Chesterfield County, VA, how the process works, and what happens if you skip it. Licensed contractor explains everything.
imgAlt: Custom deck built by MAS Contractors in Chesterfield County Virginia
excerpt: Building a deck in Chesterfield County? Here's exactly when you need a permit, what the process looks like, and the real risks of skipping it — from a licensed Virginia contractor who pulls permits every week.

content.text: Short answer: Yes. Chesterfield County requires a building permit to build, replace, add to, or structurally repair a deck, whether or not it is attached to the house. Only simple like-for-like work, such as replacing deck boards or handrails, is exempt. Here's what the county says, what the process looks like, and what skipping the permit can cost you.
When Is a Deck Permit Required in Chesterfield County?
Chesterfield's Building Inspection Department enforces the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code (USBC) and lists these deck-related projects as requiring a building permit:

items: Building a new deck or porch, including its steps or ramp, whether or not it is attached to the main structure
Replacing a deck or adding to an existing one
Making structural repairs to a deck, such as posts, beams, joists, and footings
Converting an existing deck or porch to a Florida room (sunroom)
Any deck that will carry a hot tub or spa: the county requires a design sealed by a registered design professional showing the deck can support the loads

content.text: What doesn't need a permit: the county's no-permit list includes repairing or replacing deck flooring and repairing or replacing handrails, but a permit is required to repair or replace structural elements or to include posts and guard systems. A separate electrical permit may also be required depending on the scope of work, for example for outlets or lighting. Setbacks from your property lines still apply, so the county asks for a plot plan with every deck application. When in doubt, call Chesterfield County Building Inspection at 804-751-4990, or let us handle it.
What Does the Deck Permit Process Look Like in Chesterfield?

items: Prepare a plot plan showing the deck's location, its dimensions, and its distance from every property line
Prepare two or more copies of construction plans: how the deck attaches to the house, floor framing, footing details, guardrail and picket framing, and post locations and sizes
Submit the Residential Building Permit Application with the plans, and pay the fee at application (currently $114 for a deck, plus a 2% state levy)
Chesterfield Building Inspection reviews the application
Footing inspection: the inspector checks the footings before concrete is placed (it can be combined with the final inspection if you use solid concrete block footings and leave them exposed)
Final inspection: after the deck is complete, the inspector signs off and closes the permit

content.text: MAS Contractors manages every step of this process. We prepare the drawings, submit the application, and schedule the inspections.
How Long Does Chesterfield Permit Approval Take?

Chesterfield County's published goal is to review residential plans within 10 working days, according to its residential requirements pamphlet. Actual timing depends on how complete your plans are and on the project, so we submit full drawings and build review time into every schedule. A deck that needs a sealed design, such as one carrying a hot tub, can take longer. Confirm current timing with Building Inspection.

content.text: We handle permits, inspections, and all the paperwork. You just show up for the final walkthrough.
What Happens If You Skip the Permit?
This is the part contractors don't always tell you, but we will:

items: Code investigation fee: when work starts without a required permit, Chesterfield charges a fee of the greater of 25% of the permit fee or $57, on top of the normal permit fees.
Criminal penalty: under Virginia Code § 36-106, violating the building code is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $2,500, and a court can order the violation corrected.
Insurance issues: if someone is injured on an unpermitted deck, your insurer may dispute the claim. Check your policy.
Resale problems: real estate agents and home inspectors often flag unpermitted structures, and buyers can ask for a retroactive permit or a price reduction.
Safety risk: permit inspections exist to catch problems with footings and ledger connections before they are covered up. A deck failure injures people.

content.text: Pro tip: Permits protect you, not just the county. A properly permitted and inspected deck gives you legal documentation that it was built to code — which is worth real money at resale.
Who Is Responsible for Pulling the Permit?

Chesterfield allows the property owner, a licensed contractor, or the owner's agent (with the owner's written permission) to apply for a residential permit. Virginia law lets homeowners do work on their own primary residence themselves, but we recommend a licensed contractor for a structure that people will stand on. If a contractor tells you not to worry about the permit, walk away: Virginia requires every residential contract to include the contractor's assurance that they will comply with local permit, inspection, and zoning requirements. We pull every permit ourselves and stand behind the work through every inspection.

What Is Hardie Board (Fiber Cement) Siding?

James Hardie fiber cement siding is made from a blend of cement, sand, and cellulose fibers. It's formed into planks, panels, or shingles that mimic the look of wood with dramatically better durability. MAS Contractors is a certified James Hardie installer — meaning our crews are trained and tested specifically on Hardie products and installation standards.
What Is Vinyl Siding?

Vinyl siding is extruded PVC plastic formed into horizontal or vertical planks. It is one of the most widely installed siding materials in the US, primarily because of its low upfront cost. Modern vinyl has improved significantly from earlier generations, with better UV stabilizers and thicker profiles available at premium price points.

content.text: Why Hardie Board Wins in Virginia's Climate
Virginia's mix of hot, humid summers, freeze-thaw cycles in winter, and active termite populations is hard on siding. Fiber cement handles all three better than vinyl:

items: Humidity: Vinyl can warp when temperatures swing between 95°F summer days and 20°F winter nights. Fiber cement has a much lower expansion coefficient.
Freeze-thaw: Vinyl becomes brittle in sub-freezing temperatures and can crack on impact. Fiber cement remains stable.

Termites: While vinyl isn't food for termites, it's sometimes installed over OSB or wood furring that is. Hardie installed over non-organic materials eliminates termite entry points at the siding level.
Wind and hail: Richmond and Chesterfield see significant storm activity. Fiber cement holds up to hail and wind-driven debris that would dent or crack vinyl.

When Vinyl Siding Still Makes Sense

Vinyl wins on upfront cost — sometimes by 40–60%. If you're on a tight budget, flipping a property, or working on a rental where longevity matters less than first cost, premium vinyl (0.046" or thicker) is a legitimate choice. Our Recommendation for Richmond Homeowners

For a primary residence you plan to own 10+ years: Hardie board is the better long-term investment. The higher upfront cost is offset by a longer lifespan, strong resale value (fiber-cement siding replacement recouped about 114% of its cost in the 2025 Cost vs. Value report), and the fact that you're not replacing it in 20 years. Siding replacement is generally an ordinary repair that doesn't need a Chesterfield County building permit, but structural repairs found underneath do.

title: How to Choose a General Contractor in Richmond, VA: 7 Questions to Ask
metaTitle: How to Choose a Contractor in Richmond VA | MAS Contractors Guide
metaDescription: Hiring a general contractor in Richmond VA? Ask these 7 questions before signing anything. A licensed Class A contractor explains what separates great contractors from risky ones.
imgAlt: MAS Contractors team on a residential remodeling project in Richmond Virginia
excerpt: The wrong contractor can turn your dream remodel into a nightmare. Before you sign anything or hand over a deposit, ask every Richmond contractor these 7 questions — and know what the right answers look like.

content.text: Virginia has thousands of licensed contractors and an unknown number of unlicensed ones. The difference between a great experience and a horror story almost always comes down to who you hired and what you didn't ask before signing. Here's the framework we'd want our own family members to use.
1. Are You Licensed in Virginia — and at What Class?

Virginia requires contractors to hold a license from the Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation (DPOR) for work over $1,000. The class depends on the value of the contract: Class C for a single contract over $1,000 and under $30,000, Class B from $30,000 up to $150,000, and Class A for $150,000 or more (or $1 million or more of work in a 12-month period). Make sure the contractor's class covers your job: contracting without the proper class for the value of the work is a Class 1 misdemeanor under Virginia law. You can verify any contractor's license on the DPOR website in a couple of minutes. MAS Contractors holds a Class A General Contractor License.
2. Do You Carry General Liability and Workers' Compensation Insurance?

Ask for a Certificate of Insurance — a legitimate contractor will send it without hesitation. General liability protects your property if something is damaged. Workers' compensation protects you if a worker is injured on your property (without it, you could be liable). Both are non-negotiable.
3. Do You Pull the Permits, or Do You Ask Me To?

Red flag: any contractor who asks you to pull the permit yourself as a homeowner, or suggests you skip it entirely. Virginia lets owners do work on their own primary residence, so a homeowner can apply for a permit, but then you, not a licensed contractor, answer for the work. When a licensed contractor pulls the permit, they furnish proof of their license to the building department, and Virginia requires every residential contract to include the contractor's assurance that they will comply with local permit, inspection, and zoning requirements.
4. Can You Provide References from Jobs in the Richmond Area?

Ask for 3 references from projects completed in the last 12 months, in the same neighborhood or city if possible. Call them. Ask: Did they finish on time? Were there surprises in the final bill? Would you hire them again? A great contractor will give you references enthusiastically.
5. What Does Your Payment Schedule Look Like?

Virginia requires the written contract to include the progress-payment schedule and a specific statement of the down payment amount. In our experience, legitimate contractors ask for a deposit (typically 10–33% depending on project size) with progress payments tied to completion milestones, and a final payment only after the work is done and you're satisfied. A request for more than half up front is a warning sign. Full payment before the job starts is how scams begin.
6. Will You Use Subcontractors, and Are They Licensed?

Most general contractors use subcontractors for specialized trades (HVAC, electrical, plumbing). That's normal. What you need to know is whether the subs are licensed for their trade in Virginia and covered under the GC's insurance. Ask for confirmation in writing.
7. Will I Receive a Written Contract?

Never hire a contractor based on a verbal agreement or a one-page proposal. Virginia requires residential contractors to use a legible written contract, signed by both parties before work starts or payments are accepted, and to give you a fully executed copy before work begins. At minimum it must state: when work begins and the estimated completion date; the total cost; the progress-payment schedule and the down payment; the materials and work specified; the cancellation rights of both parties; the contractor's name, address, license number, class, and specialties; that any change to cost, materials, work, or completion date must be in writing and signed by all parties; the contractor's assurance of compliance with local permit, inspection, and zoning requirements; and a notice about the Virginia Contractor Transaction Recovery Fund. If a contractor resists putting things in writing, walk away.

content.text: What Shortens Roof Life in Virginia's Climate?

items: High humidity: Richmond's humid climate promotes algae, moss, and lichen growth — particularly on north-facing slopes. These organisms don't just stain; the root systems break down shingle granules over time.
Heat cycling: Summer attic temperatures run far above the outdoor temperature. This causes asphalt shingles to expand, contract, and age faster — especially if attic ventilation is inadequate.
Ice dams: While Richmond winters are milder than further north, ice dams can still form during cold snaps. Poor attic insulation and ventilation are the root causes.
Storm damage: Richmond-area summers bring frequent thunderstorms, and the wind and occasional hail they carry wear on shingles over time.
Poor installation: Improperly driven nails, inadequate underlayment, and missing drip edge are common in budget work and can void manufacturer warranties.

items: Your roof is 20+ years old and was installed with 3-tab shingles

Interior water stains on ceilings, especially after the first freeze-thaw cycle of winter

In Chesterfield County, re-roofing and shingle replacement are on the county's list of work that does not require a permit, but structural repairs, such as damaged rafters, do. Virginia's building code also exempts replacing an unlimited amount of roof covering on houses, with a wind-speed condition, and replacing up to 256 square feet of roof decking. Best Time of Year to Replace a Roof in Richmond

Late summer and fall (August–November) are the sweet spot for roof replacements in the Richmond area. Shingle sealant strips are heat-activated, and manufacturers such as Owens Corning publish special procedures for installing shingles at or below 40°F because they may not seal right away. Dry fall weather also reduces the risk of rain delays, and shingles installed in fall have the full winter to seal before the next storm season.

Spring (March–May) is also excellent. Avoid mid-summer installations if possible — 95°F+ temperatures are hard on roofing crews and can cause asphalt shingles to distort during installation if handled improperly.

Pro tip: If you have architectural shingles with an algae-resistance rating, look for the 'AR' designation. Check the manufacturer's warranty terms for the AR rating on the product you choose — it can be worth the small premium for north-facing or heavily shaded roofs in the Richmond area.

When Is a Permit Required for a Home Addition in Chesterfield County?

Chesterfield's list of projects that require a building permit includes building an addition onto an existing house or attached garage, converting a garage to a habitable space, converting a deck or porch to a Florida room, finishing off an unfinished attic, basement, or room over a garage, and moving, adding, or removing a wall. Second-story additions
In-law suites built as part of the house

content.text: Do You Need an Architect or Engineer for a Home Addition?

Not always. Virginia law does not require an architect or engineer license for the person who prepares plans for single- and two-family homes of up to three stories (Code of Virginia § 54.1-402), and Chesterfield's own guidance says drawings may be prepared by the homeowner or contractor and that a registered architect or engineer is not required for most single-family dwellings. Some items do need an engineer, though. The county requires a sealed soil report showing shrink-swell potential for additions with habitable space in the Triassic basin, and an engineered footing where that potential is moderate or higher. Full-height two-story walls over 12 feet must be engineered by a registered design professional. imgAlt: Bathroom remodel in Richmond, VA by MAS Contractors — freestanding tub with large-format marble-veined tile and basketweave mosaic floor
excerpt: "How much will my bathroom remodel cost?" is the single most-searched question in home remodeling. Here are real 2026 numbers for the Richmond area — broken down by scope, by line item, and by the surprises that actually blow up budgets.

content.text: Bathroom remodeling is the most-searched home improvement category in the country, and "how much does it cost" is the question behind almost all of it. The honest answer is that the same 40-square-foot bathroom can cost $8,000 or $38,000 depending on three things: whether the plumbing moves, what goes on the walls and floor, and what's hiding under the old subfloor. Here's how that breaks down across Richmond, North Chesterfield, and Henrico.
Bathroom Remodel Cost by Scope in Richmond, VA

rows: New vanity, toilet, fixtures, lighting, paint — nothing moves
Full tear-out, new tile floor and shower surround, vanity, fixtures, same layout
Custom tile work, walk-in shower, double vanity, some plumbing relocation
Freestanding tub, frameless glass, heated floors, full layout change

content.text: The ranges above come from our own projects in the Richmond area: our typical full remodel averages $12,000 to $22,000. Your price depends mostly on whether the plumbing moves, what goes on the walls and floor, and what we find under the old subfloor.
Where the Money Actually Goes
Most homeowners assume materials are the biggest line item. They usually aren't. On a typical bathroom remodel the split looks like this:

rows: Licensed trades run $85–$120/hr; tile setting and plumbing are the most labor-dense phases
Tile, vanity, fixtures, glass, backer board, waterproofing membrane
Permit fees, dumpster, protection, unforeseen repairs

content.text: This is why the cheapest bid is so often the most expensive outcome. Labor is roughly half the job, so a contractor who is dramatically cheaper than everyone else is usually cutting hours somewhere — and in a bathroom, the hours that get cut are almost always waterproofing and substrate prep, the two things you cannot see once the tile goes on.
Common Line Items and What They Cost

items: Tile, installed: $8–$30+ per square foot depending on material and pattern. A full bathroom floor and shower typically runs $3,000–$12,000.
Double vanity with quartz or granite top: $2,500–$6,000 installed for mid-range.
Heated floor system: $500–$1,500. Dramatically cheaper to add during a remodel than after — if the floor is already coming up, this is the moment to decide.
Updated lighting: roughly $400–$800 with labor to replace a fluorescent vanity bar with LED fixtures on a dimmer.

Moving a drain or relocating plumbing: this is the single biggest swing factor. Keeping the toilet, shower, and vanity in their existing locations can save several thousand dollars versus a layout change.

content.text: Richmond-Specific Cost Factors

Three things drive bathroom budgets up in this market more than anywhere else, and all three are age-related. Richmond has a large stock of homes built well before 1990, and bathrooms are where that age shows up first.

items: Hidden subfloor rot: A bathroom that has had a slow leak around the toilet flange or shower pan for years will have compromised subfloor underneath. You don't find it until demo day. Budget a contingency — this is the most common bathroom surprise we encounter.

Lead or galvanized supply lines in older homes: lead pipes, solder, and flux were banned for drinking-water plumbing by the 1986 Safe Drinking Water Act amendments, so homes built before then may have lead or galvanized supply piping. Have a licensed plumber check them; replacing old supply lines during a remodel is often the sensible time to do it.

Undersized ventilation: The International Residential Code, which the Virginia Residential Code is based on, sets a minimum bathroom exhaust of 50 cfm for a fan run intermittently (20 cfm if run continuously). Many older fans fall short or are poorly ducted, so we often recommend a quiet, ENERGY STAR fan sized to the room and ducted outdoors. Upgrading is inexpensive, but it's a line item most budget estimates leave out entirely.

content.text: Permits: in Chesterfield County, a permit is required if the remodel installs new piping or fixtures or relocates fixtures, involves electrical wiring beyond swapping a fixture, or changes anything structural. The county's no-permit list includes replacing plumbing fixtures like sinks, toilets, and faucets and installing new floor coverings, so purely cosmetic work in the same locations generally does not need one. In Chesterfield, fees are flat: a renovation with no change in square footage carries a $114 building permit, and plumbing and electrical permits run $57 to $114 each, plus a 2% state levy. Henrico and the City of Richmond have their own offices and fee schedules. We pull all required permits as part of the project scope.

Where You Can Save — and Where You Shouldn't
There are real ways to bring a bathroom budget down without ending up with a bathroom you regret:

items: Save: Keep the existing layout. Not moving plumbing is the single biggest lever you control.
Save: Use large-format porcelain instead of natural stone. It costs less, needs no sealing, holds up better in humidity, and makes a small bathroom look larger with fewer grout lines.
Save: Reglaze or keep a tub that's structurally fine rather than replacing it, if a tub still fits your plans.
Don't skimp: Waterproofing. Cement backer board plus a proper membrane, never greenboard. Greenboard is moisture-resistant, not waterproof, and it will eventually fail behind a shower.
Don't skimp: The exhaust fan. An undersized fan is how you get mold and peeling paint in a brand-new bathroom.

content.text: How Long Does a Bathroom Remodel Take?

A standard bathroom remodel takes 2 to 3 weeks. A full master bath with custom tile runs 4 to 5 weeks. Tile work alone — substrate prep, waterproofing, setting, grouting — accounts for 4 to 6 days of that, and it cannot be compressed without compromising the installation. We provide a written schedule before demo begins.

If your priority is resale rather than daily enjoyment, the math changes — a strategic refresh often beats a full gut on percentage return. We covered that in detail in our guide to bathroom remodel ROI in Richmond.

Pro tip: set and inspect the rough plumbing before a single tile goes down. Moving a drain after the floor is tiled means tearing the whole floor back out — a $3,000+ mistake that's completely avoidable with one inspection at the right moment.

excerpt: "How much does a deck cost?" is the first question every homeowner asks — and the honest answer depends on size, material, and how many features get added along the way. Here are real 2026 numbers for the Richmond area, broken down by what actually drives the price.

content.text: A deck is one of the few home improvements where the price can double from a simple design change, not a material swap. The same 200-square-foot footprint can run $6,000 or $20,000 depending on whether it's single-level pressure-treated pine or a multi-level composite build with built-in seating. Here's how that breaks down across Richmond, North Chesterfield, and Henrico.
Deck Cost by Size and Material in Richmond, VA

rows: Single-level platform, standard railing, one set of stairs
Larger footprint, standard railing, stairs to grade
Composite boards over pressure-treated framing, same footprint
Multiple levels, built-in seating or lighting, larger footprint

content.text: Our typical Richmond-area project lands between $12,000 and $22,000.
Where the Money Actually Goes
Unlike a kitchen or bathroom, a deck's budget is weighted toward materials rather than labor, especially once composite decking enters the picture:

rows: Decking boards, framing lumber, railing, hardware, footings
Excavation, footings, framing, decking installation, railing and finish work
Permit fees, disposal, and any substrate or ledger repairs found on site

content.text: Common Line Items and What They Cost

items: Composite decking upgrade over pressure-treated boards: adds roughly $15–$25 per square foot, but eliminates the annual sanding and staining a wood deck needs.
Built-in bench seating: $800–$2,000 depending on length and material.
Deck lighting (post caps, step lights, low-voltage system): $500–$1,500.
Screened-in porch conversion or roof addition: $8,000–$20,000+, the single biggest add-on we build.
Stairs to grade: roughly $150–$300 per step installed, more for wide or curved stairs.
Cable or glass-panel railing instead of standard balusters: adds $30–$60 per linear foot.

content.text: Richmond-Specific Cost Factors
Three things move deck budgets in this market that don't show up in a national cost calculator.

items: Footing depth: Chesterfield County's deck design guide calls for footings that bear on undisturbed soil 18 to 20 inches below finished grade, and at least as deep as the house footing when a deck footing sits within 4 feet of the house. That adds excavation cost homeowners moving from warmer climates rarely expect.

Sloped lots: a lot of Richmond-area backyards slope away from the house. A deck that looks like a simple rectangle from the street often needs a taller substructure or a multi-level design once we're on site measuring.

HOA and historic-district review: some Chesterfield and Henrico neighborhoods require material and color approval before a permit can be pulled. It doesn't change the build cost, but it can add one to two weeks to the timeline.

content.text: Permits: in Chesterfield County, a building permit is required to build a deck whether or not it is attached to the house, which covers every deck we build. The deck permit fee is currently $114 plus a 2% state levy. We cover exactly when a permit applies, and what the process looks like, in our guide to deck permits in Chesterfield County. We pull all required permits as part of the project scope.

content.text: We walk your yard, check the grade and access, and give you a detailed line-item quote — so you know exactly where every dollar goes before we start.
Where You Can Save — and Where You Shouldn't

items: Save: Keep the deck single-level and rectangular. Multi-level designs and curved edges add framing complexity that shows up directly in labor hours.
Save: Pressure-treated lumber for the substructure under composite decking boards — you get the low-maintenance surface without paying composite prices for framing nobody sees.
Save: Standard baluster railing instead of cable or glass. It's a fraction of the cost and, built to the details in the county's deck guide, meets code.
Don't skimp: Footings. Undersized or shallow footings are the number one reason a deck starts to sag or pull away from the house within a few years.
Don't skimp: Ledger board attachment. This single connection holds the entire deck to your house — it has to be properly flashed and lag-bolted into the house's framing, not just the siding.

content.text: How Long Does a Deck Build Take?

A standard single-level deck (200–300 square feet) typically takes 1 to 2 weeks to build once permits are approved. A larger multi-level deck, or one with a screened porch or roof addition, can run 3 to 4 weeks. Chesterfield County's published goal is to review residential plans within 10 working days, so most homeowners should plan on 4 to 8 weeks from signed contract to finished deck.

Pro tip: order your composite decking as soon as the contract is signed. Popular colors from major manufacturers can have 4–6 week lead times during peak season (spring and early summer) — material lead time controls your start date far more often than the crew's schedule does.

title: Do I Need a Permit for a Roof Replacement or Siding in Chesterfield County, VA?
metaTitle: Roof & Siding Permit Chesterfield County VA | MAS Contractors
metaDescription: Do you need a permit to replace a roof or siding in Chesterfield County, VA? What Virginia's building code and the county say, and when a permit is required.
imgAlt: Roof replacement project completed by MAS Contractors in Chesterfield County, Virginia
excerpt: Most homeowners are surprised to learn that a like-for-like roof or siding replacement usually doesn't need a building permit in Chesterfield County. But "usually" has exceptions. Here's what Virginia's building code and the county actually say, and the cases where a permit is required.

content.text: Short answer: usually no. Under Virginia's building code, replacing your existing roof covering or siding on a house is treated as an ordinary repair, and Chesterfield County lists re-roofing and siding among the work that does not need a permit. But a handful of situations flip that answer to yes: structural repairs, a large amount of roof decking, asbestos-containing materials, and certain historic or flood-zone properties.
What Does Virginia Law Say About Roof and Siding Permits?

Building permits in Virginia come from the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code (USBC), which every locality enforces through its own building department (Code of Virginia § 36-105). Section 108.1 of the USBC says a permit is required for the construction or demolition of a building and for alterations involving any structural component, among other things. Section 108.2 then lists work that is exempt, including a category called ordinary repairs.

Two items in that list matter here. First, the code exempts "replacement of an unlimited amount of roof covering or siding" on one- and two-family homes and townhouses, provided the building is not in an area where the nominal design wind speed is greater than 100 mph. Second, it exempts replacing 256 square feet or less of roof decking on those same buildings, unless the decking was originally required to be fire-retardant-treated or otherwise protected as part of a fire-rated assembly.

content.alt: Roofing crew installing new cedar shingles on a historic stone house with scaffolding around it
content.caption: A crew installs new cedar shingles on a historic stone house. Replacing the roof covering is an ordinary repair; replacing structural framing is not.
content.credit: Photo: NPS, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

content.text: What Does Chesterfield County Say?

Chesterfield's Building Inspection Department enforces the USBC and says a building permit is required for most work on your home, "except for some ordinary or minor repairs." Its list of residential work that does not require a permit includes repairing siding, re-roofing and shingles, painting the inside or outside of the house, and installing or replacing gutters and downspouts. Its project requirements page puts installing vinyl siding under cosmetic changes and reroofing under ordinary repairs.
The same pages are just as clear on the other side: any work that is structural in nature requires a permit.
Roof and Siding Permit Rules at a Glance

rows: Tear-off and new shingles, metal, or other roof covering
Roof covering replacement is an ordinary repair under USBC § 108.2
Replacing siding (vinyl, fiber cement, wood) on a house
Siding replacement is an ordinary repair; the county lists it as no-permit work
Replacing up to 256 sq ft of roof decking
Replacing more than 256 sq ft of roof decking
The exemption stops at 256 sq ft
Repairing or replacing rafters, trusses, beams, or wall framing
Changing the roof shape or framing a new dormer or skylight opening
Home in a locally designated historic district
USBC exception for replacement siding, roofing, and windows
Home in a special flood hazard area

content.text: When Is a Permit Required for a Roof or Siding Job?
In our experience the "yes" answers almost always come from what is found after the old material comes off, not from the plan on paper:

items: Rot in the framing: when old siding or shingles come off and the sheathing is fine, nothing changes. When rafters, trusses, or wall studs have rotted, replacing them is structural work and needs a permit.
More than 256 square feet of decking: a few bad sheets are exempt, but a roof with widespread deck damage can go past the exemption.
Asbestos-containing material: older homes can have cement-board siding or roofing that contains asbestos. Removing or disturbing it requires a permit under the USBC.

Historic districts: the building official may require a permit for replacement siding and roofing inside a locally designated historic district, and the district may have its own material and color rules.
Special flood hazard areas: the building official may require a permit for otherwise-exempt work.

content.alt: Two neighboring row houses with vinyl siding, one beige and one light gray
content.caption: Replacing siding like this is treated as an ordinary repair, unless the work uncovers structural damage.
content.credit: Photo: Cbaile19, CC0 public domain dedication, via Wikimedia Commons

content.text: Pro tip: "no permit" does not mean "no code." The USBC exemptions don't excuse the work from the code's other requirements, so flashing, underlayment, fastening, and ventilation still have to meet it, and a permit-free job also has no county inspection checking them. That is why who does the work matters more when there is no inspector.

There is one more detail worth knowing. When an owner or the owner's agent asks for a permit on exempt work, the code says a permit shall be issued and the related inspections are then required. Some homeowners ask for one on a big job for the paper trail.
How to Confirm Before You Start

items: Check whether your property is in a locally designated historic district or a special flood hazard area. Either can change the answer.
Check your HOA or subdivision covenants. They are separate from the building code and can require approval of roofing and siding materials and colors even when no county permit is needed.
Ask your contractor to inspect the roof deck and framing before quoting a fixed price, because rot and decking damage are what change the permit answer.
If anything is unclear, call Chesterfield County Building Inspection at 804-751-4990 (Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.) with your address and a short description of the work.

Who Pulls the Permit When One Is Required?

Chesterfield allows the property owner, a licensed contractor, or the owner's agent (with written permission from the owner) to apply for a residential permit. When a permit applies to your roof or siding job, your contractor should handle it as part of the scope. We do, and we schedule the inspections too.
